name: task-decomposition
description: Approach for handling tasks that won't fit in one focused work block. Break them down BEFORE starting work, not after getting stuck.

metadata.approach: If a task estimates >3hrs of focused work, decompose into ≤3hr subtasks and link via `part_of`. Each subtask should have a verifiable definition-of-done. Decompose along acceptance-criteria boundaries, not technology boundaries.
checks: each subtask has a single observable success criterion
subtasks link to the parent via part_of edge
no subtask >3hrs of focused work
the decomposition covers the parent's full acceptance criteria (no gaps)
subtasks ordered by dependency, not by interest
examples_good: Parent: 'wire memex hooks for auto-capture' (5hrs)\nSubtasks: [add observe-event CLI; add todowrite-sync CLI; add hooks-install template; smoke-test on a real session]
examples_bad: Parent: 'rebuild memex' (40hrs)\nSubtasks: [add stuff; fix things; ship it]  # vague, unverifiable, no dependency order

name: blocker-resolution
description: Approach for handling tasks that depend on external work or someone else's input.

metadata.approach: Before marking a task `blocked`, identify the SPECIFIC blocker as its own task with a `blocks` edge. 'Blocked on Bob' is not a blocker — 'Bob to confirm cors policy by Friday' is. The blocker task carries the owner and due date.
checks: the blocker exists as its own concrete task with an owner and a due date
a `blocks` edge connects blocker → blocked
the blocked task's status is set to `blocked`
if the blocker is external (vendor, third party), there's a follow-up plan if they don't respond by the due date
examples_good: task A: 'integrate Stripe MCP' status=blocked\nlink: task B blocks task A\ntask B: 'Stripe to enable Restricted Keys for org' owner=stripe-support due=2026-05-12
examples_bad: task A: 'integrate Stripe MCP' status=blocked  # no blocker recorded — when it unblocks, no one knows

name: definition-of-done
description: Approach for declaring a task complete. Hidden incompletes are the slow leak that ruins project memory.

metadata.approach: A task's status moves to `completed` (and confidence to 1.0) ONLY when its acceptance criteria are observable and observed. 'I think it works' is not done. 'Tests pass / endpoint returns 200 / user confirmed / metric shows expected value' is done. If completion isn't verifiable, the task wasn't well-defined.
checks: acceptance criteria were stated when the task was created (or are added before marking done)
each criterion has been observed (test ran, endpoint hit, user confirmed)
if completion changed shared state (deployed code, schema migration), the change is reflected somewhere recall() can find it
tasks blocked by this one are reviewed and possibly unblocked
examples_good: update_task(id=t1, status='completed') only after: pytest passes locally + CI green + manual smoke test of the new CLI command
examples_bad: update_task(id=t1, status='completed') because 'the code looks right' — no test, no smoke check

name: weekly-review
description: Approach for periodic memex hygiene. Without it, the task graph slowly fills with stale items that lie about your real backlog.

metadata.approach: Once a week, list_tasks(status='*') and for each: confirm status (anything in_progress that hasn't moved in >7 days is probably done or abandoned — close it), confirm priority (does p1 from 3 weeks ago still feel like p1?), close stale tasks rather than leaving them open. Run progress() to capture what was done.
checks: every task with status=in_progress has been touched in the last 7 days; if not, decide: completed, blocked, or cancelled
every task with priority=p0 or p1 still belongs at that priority; demote if not
tasks with status=blocked have a current blocker (the blocker task isn't itself stale)
completed tasks from this week are noted (so progress() reflects real velocity)
examples_good: Friday: list_tasks(status='in_progress') → 4 tasks; 1 hasn't moved in 11 days → update_task(status='cancelled', description+='cancelled during weekly review: scope abandoned')
examples_bad: never doing it; the in_progress count grows monotonically and stops being meaningful

name: task-from-correction
description: Approach for capturing follow-up work when the user corrects you. Don't lose the lesson.

metadata.approach: When the user corrects an assumption you made, BEFORE moving on: (1) observe(kind='user_correction', payload={rule, why}) to record the event; (2) if the correction implies durable knowledge, add_node(kind='constraint' or 'decision') with the rule + Why; (3) if the correction implies follow-up work, add_task() with priority p1 and link spawned_from the correction event. All three.
checks: the correction is recorded as an episodic event
if it's a durable rule, it's also a concept (constraint/decision) findable via recall
if it implies follow-up, a task exists for it (otherwise it's lost)
the next session can find this correction by recalling the relevant topic
examples_good: user: 'never use --no-verify on commits' → observe(kind='user_correction', payload={...}) + add_node(kind='constraint', name='no --no-verify on commits', description='**Why:** bypasses pre-commit hooks (lint/type-check)\n**How to apply:** if hooks fail, fix the issue or ask the user, never bypass')
examples_bad: just internalizing the correction within the session and not recording it — the next session repeats the mistake
